reason: The sources corroborate dozens of multi-source claims detailing Iapetus's discovery, walnut shape, 12-mile-high equatorial ridge, two-faced coloration, and thermal runaway.
story: In 1671, astronomer Giovanni Domenico Cassini spotted a new moon orbiting Saturn, but there was a catch: it completely vanished for half of its orbit. Cassini deduced the truth: the moon, Iapetus, is tidally locked and split into two drastically different hemispheres—one bright as ice, the other pitch-black. When modern spacecraft arrived, they found Iapetus was even stranger than Cassini imagined. Orbiting far out on an inclined plane, it offers the only front-row view of Saturn's rings among major moons. Stranger still, running three-quarters of the way around its equator is a colossal mountain ridge soaring up to 12 miles high, making the moon look like a giant walnut. Scientists discovered that dark dust swept from outer moons absorbs sunlight, heating the surface and boiling away ice into cold zones, cementing the extreme two-tone contrast while leaving the origin of its towering equatorial ridge an unsolved mystery.
angle: A colossal 12-mile-high mountain ridge runs directly along the equator of Iapetus, turning this two-toned world into a giant cosmic walnut.

claims.claim: Iapetus was discovered by astronomer Giovanni Domenico Cassini in 1671.
Iapetus is the third-largest moon of Saturn.
Iapetus is tidally locked to Saturn, keeping the same face pointed at the planet.
Iapetus has a slow orbital and rotational period of approximately 79 days.
Iapetus exhibits a striking contrast between a dark leading hemisphere and a bright trailing hemisphere.
The dark hemisphere of Iapetus has an albedo of 0.03 to 0.05, while the bright hemisphere has an albedo of 0.5 to 0.6.
John Herschel suggested naming the moons of Saturn after mythological Titans.
Geological features on Iapetus are named after characters and places from the French epic poem The Song of Roland.
Cassini initially labeled Iapetus as Saturn V, and it eventually became designated as Saturn VIII.
Iapetus has an inclined orbit, making it the only large moon from which Saturn's rings would be clearly visible rather than edge-on.
Iapetus is composed primarily of water ice with only about 20 to 25 percent rocky material.
An equatorial ridge encircles most of the equator of Iapetus, giving the moon the appearance of a walnut.
Peaks along the equatorial ridge rise up to 20 kilometers (12 miles) above the surrounding plains.
The equatorial ridge was discovered in images taken by the Cassini spacecraft on December 31, 2004.
In the bright region of Iapetus, the continuous ridge breaks down into a series of isolated 10-kilometer-high peaks.
The equatorial ridge is heavily cratered, indicating that it is an ancient geological feature.
The dark material on Iapetus is a thin veneer only about a foot (a few tens of centimeters) thick in some areas, through which small meteor impacts punch into underlying ice.
A thermal segregation runaway process causes heated dark areas to lose ice by sublimation, which then condenses in colder bright regions.
The Cassini spacecraft completed a targeted close flyby of Iapetus in September 2007 at an altitude of approximately 1,227 to 1,229 kilometers.
Iapetus is host to massive, long-runout landslides known as sturzstroms.
The largest impact basin on Iapetus is Turgis, spanning roughly 580 kilometers (360 miles) across.

disputed: Which hemisphere is dark versus bright: S1, S3, S4, and S5 state the leading hemisphere is dark and trailing is bright, whereas S7 mistakenly claims the trailing side is dark and leading is bright. The script should follow the scientific consensus that the leading hemisphere is dark.

Which side of Saturn Cassini first saw Iapetus on: S1, S3, and S4 note Cassini saw it on the western side and it disappeared on the eastern side, while S7 claims he saw it on the eastern side and it vanished on the western side. The script should follow the historical consensus from S1, S3, and S4.

The origin of the equatorial ridge: hypotheses include remnant rotational flattening from early rapid spin, de-orbiting of an ancient ring system or shattered moonlet, cryovolcanic upwelling, and convective overturn. The script should present the origin as an unsolved mystery with competing theories.

The origin of the initial dark coating: external debris swept up from outer retrograde moons such as Phoebe versus internal cryovolcanic eruptions of hydrocarbons. The script should present both external accretion and internal activity as proposed origins.
